1. Core Clinical Tension: An elderly Caribbean-born woman presenting with dramatic cachexia (25-lb weight loss), anorexia, altered stool caliber, and postoperative bowel pseudo-obstruction with absent peripheral eosinophilia, creating high suspicion for an occult gastrointestinal malignancy or acute mechanical postoperative obstruction while disguising a severe intestinal helminthic infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is set at admission emergency triage following abdominal radiography, CT, upper GI follow-through, and tumor marker profiling, prior to repeat upper endoscopy with mucosal biopsy and formal stool ova and parasite testing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Advanced gastrointestinal malignancy or mechanical bowel obstruction was ruled out by negative serum tumor markers, absence of discrete focal mass or transition point on CT, and histological identification of Strongyloides stercoralis worms within duodenal mucosal crypts.
case_prompt:
A 74-year-old female retired home healthcare worker presents with severe epigastric abdominal pain and vomiting developing after a left inguinal hernia repair performed 7 days earlier. Her symptoms began 2 days post-procedure as severe, burning, non-radiating epigastric pain accompanied by low-grade fever, nausea, postprandial clear and mucoid vomiting, and obstipation. Over the preceding 6 months, she had experienced anorexia, altered stool caliber, progressive malaise, and an unintentional weight loss of 25 pounds in a single month. An outpatient esophagogastroduodenoscopy performed 4 months prior for similar symptoms was reported as normal. She resides in rural Grenada for 6 months each year, where she cultivates and eats her own home-grown vegetables, and spends the remainder of the year in the United States. She denies alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs, and reports no history of pruritus or rash. Past surgical history includes umbilical hernia repair, hysterectomy in 2012, and left inguinal hernia repair in 2015.
On examination, she appears fatigued, apathetic, and malnourished. Vital signs: blood pressure 135/90 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, temperature 99.8°F, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft and nondistended, with tenderness to light and deep palpation in the umbilical area, without palpable masses or organomegaly. Bowel sounds are normoactive. The left inguinal surgical site is tender with mild swelling but no drainage.
Laboratory evaluation reveals a total white blood cell count of 11,000/mm³ with a completely normal absolute eosinophil count and percentage. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, and CA-125) are within normal limits. Abdominal radiography and CT scan show gastric dilation and generalized small bowel distention up to 4.5 cm in diameter consistent with ileus, without an identifiable mechanical transition point, masses, or lymphadenopathy. Upper gastrointestinal follow-through demonstrates jejunal mural thickening with loss of the normal mucosal fold pattern, suggesting extensive enteritis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Rapid profound unintentional weight loss (25 lbs), anorexia, altered stool caliber, and jejunal mural thickening raised high clinical suspicion for gastrointestinal carcinoma or lymphoma; however, CT showed no discrete mass or lymphadenopathy, and tumor markers were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Tumor markers for CA-19-9, CEA, and CA-125 were also measured and were within normal limits to rule out malignancy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Obstipation, persistent vomiting, and small bowel distension occurring days after inguinal hernia repair suggested mechanical obstruction or incarcerated hernia; however, CT demonstrated generalized dilation up to 4.5 cm consistent with ileus without an identifiable mechanical transition point.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: suggested evidence of ileus and dilated stomach with small bowel distended up to 4.5 cm diameter without identifiable obstruction

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Repeat upper endoscopy showing mucosal erythema and duodenal/gastric biopsies revealing numerous parasitic sections of Strongyloides stercoralis within glandular crypts, confirmed by stool ova and parasite examination demonstrating rhabditiform larvae.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Microscopic examination samples in the nonfundic type of gastric mucosal biopsy showed numerous parasites in the lumen of the glands (Figures 1 and 2). Parasite sections were noted in cross-sectional views and in other areas showing in long sections, which were identified as Strongyloides stercoralis.

editor_comments: Case prompt strictly adheres to admission breakpoint before endoscopic biopsy and stool microscopy. Zero mentions of Strongyloides or helminthic infestation.
